text:
Chapter Two Characteristics Associated with Autism Although every person with autism is unique, some characteristics are considered particularly important in the diagnosis. These fall into four major categories: communication social interaction unusual behaviour learning Other characteristics of behaviour and learning can be categorized as: unusual patterns of attention unusual responses to sensory stimuli anxiety This chapter addresses these seven categories and outlines instructional implications for each. 1. Communication All people with autism experience language and communication difficulties, although there are considerable differences in ability. Some are non-verbal while others may have extensive language with deficits in  pragmatics  (the social use of language). People with autism may seem caught up in a private world in which communication is unimportant.  This is not an intentional action but rather an inability to communicate. Language difficulties that may be present include: Non-verbal communication difficulties:  inappropriate facial expressions, unusual use of gestures, lack of eye contact, strange body postures, lack of mutual or shared focus of attention Delay in or lack of  expressive language skills Differences in oral language  (for those who develop it): odd pitch or intonation; faster or slower rate than normal; unusual rhythm or stress; monotone or lilting voice quality Repetitive and idiosyncratic  speech patterns Echolalia  — immediate or delayed literal repetition of the speech of others. It:
     appears to be non-meaningful, but may indicate an attempt to communicate indicates the ability to produce speech and to imitate may serve a communication or cognitive purpose for the student Restricted vocabulary:  dominated by nouns; often confined to requests or rejections to regulate one's physical environment; limited in social functions Perseveration  — a tendency to continually discuss one topic and have difficulty changing topics Difficulty with the pragmatics of conversation:  problems initiating; difficulty using unwritten rules; inability to maintain conversation on a topic; inappropriate interrupting; inflexible, stereotypic style of speaking "The student may be using echolalic utterances to rehearse what is heard in order to process the information, or as a strategy for self-regulation." — B. Prizant & J. Duchan, "The functions of immediate echolalia in autistic children," 1981 People with autism often have difficulty comprehending verbal information, following long verbal instructions, and remembering a sequence of instructions. Comprehension may be context-specific. Even those with normal intelligence (usually called high-functioning) may have difficulty with comprehension of verbal information. Implications for instruction Effective programs include comprehensive communication assessment and intervention — typically assessment by a speech and language pathologist plus informal observation and classroom-based evaluation. This forms the basis for goals, objectives, and strategies for receptive and expressive language, particularly pragmatic skills. Instruction should emphasize  paying attention, imitating, comprehending, and using language in play and social interaction . Communication goals should emphasize the  functional use  of language in various settings. 2. Social interaction Students with autism demonstrate qualitative differences in social interaction and often have difficulty establishing relationships. They may have limited social interactions or a rigid way of interacting with others. These difficulties  should not be seen as a lack of interest or unwillingness  to interact; they may result from an inability to distill social information from the interaction and use appropriate communication skills to respond. "One must separate the variables of social interaction problems from emotions. People with autism desire emotional contact with other people but they are stymied by complex social interaction." — Temple Grandin,  Thinking in Pictures , 1995, p. 44 Understanding social situations requires language processing and non-verbal communication, which are often areas of deficit. People with autism may not notice important social cues, and may miss necessary information. They typically have impairment in using non-verbal behaviours and gestures to regulate social interaction, and may have difficulty reading the non-verbal behaviour of others. They have significant difficulty with any interaction that requires knowledge of other people and what they think or know. Baron-Cohen has described this as a deficit in  theory of mind : people with autism may not be able to understand the perspective of others, or even that other people have a perspective different from their own. They may also have difficulty understanding their own — and particularly others' — beliefs, desires, intentions, knowledge, and perceptions. For example, a child with autism may not understand that another child is sad, even if that child is crying, because they are not themselves sad. Students with autism show these difficulties in observable ways: playing with toys and objects in unusual and stereotypical ways; excessive or inappropriate laughing or giggling; play that lacks imaginative, social qualities; playing near others without sharing or taking turns; or withdrawing entirely from social situations. Social interaction occurs on a continuum, with three subtypes: Subtype Description Aloof No observable interest in interacting with others except to satisfy basic needs; may become agitated in close proximity to others and reject unsolicited physical or social contact. Passive Does not initiate social approaches, but will accept initiations from others. Active but odd Approaches others for social interaction, but in an unusual and often inappropriate fashion. People with autism do not necessarily fall into one distinct spot on the continuum. Implications for instruction Social skill development is essential and is an important component in plans for managing challenging behaviours. Students with autism  do not learn social skills incidentally  by observation and participation. It is generally necessary to target specific skills for explicit instruction and to provide support for using them in social situations. (See  Strategies for teaching social skills .) 3. Unusual behaviour People with autism often demonstrate unusual and distinctive behaviours, including: restricted range of interests, and preoccupation with one specific interest or object inflexible adherence to a non-functional routine stereotypic and repetitive motor mannerisms — hand flapping, finger flicking, rocking, spinning, walking on tiptoes, spinning objects preoccupation with parts of objects fascination with movement, such as a spinning fan or turning wheels on toys insistence on sameness and resistance to change unusual responses to sensory stimuli Implications for instruction Many of these behaviours may be caused by other factors: hyper- or hypo-sensitivity to sensory stimulation, difficulty understanding social situations, difficulty with changes in routine, and anxiety. The plan should include strategies for expanding interests, developing skills, understanding sensory responses, and preparing the student for planned changes. Consider the problem behaviour and its  function  for that child — for example, gaining attention or avoiding something. It may not be possible to eliminate all repetitive behaviours. Successful strategies often focus on  environmental adaptations  to decrease an inappropriate behaviour, and/or teaching a  more appropriate behaviour that serves the same function . 4. Learning People with autism have a psycho-educational profile different from typically developing individuals. There may be deficits in many cognitive functions, yet not all are affected; complex abilities may be impaired while simpler abilities in the same area are intact. Research identifies these cognitive features: deficits in paying attention to relevant cues and information, and in attending to multiple cues receptive and expressive language impairments, particularly using language to express abstract concepts deficits in concept formation and abstract reasoning impairment in social cognition — sharing attention and emotion with others, and understanding others' feelings inability to plan, organize, and solve problems Some students have stronger abilities in  rote memory and visual-spatial tasks . They may excel at puzzles and perform well at spatial, perceptual, and matching tasks. Some may recall simple information but have difficulty recalling more complex information. "When I was a child and a teenager, I thought everybody thought in pictures. I had no idea that my thought processes were different." — Temple Grandin,  Thinking in Pictures , 1995, p. 20 Temple Grandin suggests that some people with autism more easily learn and remember information presented visually, and may have problems learning about things that cannot be thought about in pictures. Students may have difficulty comprehending oral and written information — following directions or understanding what they read — yet some higher-functioning individuals may identify words, apply phonetic skills, and know word meanings. Some show strength in sound production (phonology), vocabulary, and simple grammar (syntax), yet struggle with conversation and social use of speech (pragmatics). A high-functioning student may compute numbers easily yet be unable to solve math problems. Implications for instruction Cognitive development is usually  uneven . Base the education program on the individual's unique combination of strengths and needs. Given documented deficits in attention, language, concept formation, and memory for complex information — plus personal accounts of visual orientation —  incorporate visual material  when teaching. 5. Unusual patterns of attention Students often have difficulty paying attention to relevant cues and may focus only on a restricted part of the environment. For example, a student may look at the ball but not at the person to whom it is to be thrown, or notice a staple in the corner of a paper but not the information on it. This is called  stimulus over-selectivity . Another feature is an impaired capacity to share attention between two things or people —  joint attention . Students may also have difficulty disengaging and shifting attention from one stimulus to the next, which may contribute to rigidity and resistance to change. They may also have a short attention span. Implications for instruction Attention difficulties may affect social behaviour and language — e.g., responding to irrelevant cues, or attending to only part of a conversation. Present information in a format that is  clear, focuses attention, and emphasizes the most relevant information . Develop individualized strategies for focusing attention; parents can share methods that work at home. Ideally, the student eventually learns to manage these strategies independently. 6. Unusual responses to sensory stimuli Responses to sensory stimulation may range from  hyposensitivity  (under-reactive) to  hypersensitivity  (over-reactive). Environmental stimuli may be disturbing or even painful to someone with autism, for any type of sensory input. Other characteristics associated with autism may be caused, in part, by a disorder in sensory processing — so consider both the type and amount of stimulation in the environment and the individual's reaction to it. Tactile system The skin gathers information through touch, temperature, and pressure, interpreted as pain, neutral information, or pleasure. Students affected in this system may withdraw when touched ( tactile defensive ), or overreact to textures of objects, clothing, or food — which can lead to behaviour problems, irritability, or withdrawal. Some types and amounts of stimulation may instead have a calming effect. Auditory system Students may be hypo- or hypersensitive to sounds. Seemingly innocuous sounds can cause extreme responses — a problem in schools full of chair scraping, bells, intercom announcements, and machinery. People with autism report such sounds can seem excruciatingly intense. Visual and olfactory systems Some students react to odours such as perfumes and deodorants; others use smell to explore their surroundings in unexpected ways. Some cover their eyes to avoid certain lighting, reflections, or shiny objects, while others seek out shiny things and look at them for long periods. "As I walk down the street, I know what everyone is having for dinner by the smells coming from the houses." — A 14-year-old boy with Asperger's syndrome Vestibular and proprioceptive systems The inner ear detects movement and changes in position. Students may be fearful of movement and have trouble on stairs or ramps, seeming strangely fearful or clumsy — or the opposite, actively seeking intense movement like whirling and spinning. Students who have trouble integrating information from muscles and body parts may have odd posture and appear clumsy. Implications for instruction Aversive sensory experiences may contribute to inappropriate behaviours. People with severe sensory processing problems may shut down to avoid over-stimulation;  tantrums may be related to escaping over-stimulating situations ; self-stimulating behaviours may help the individual calm down by generating a self-controlled, repetitive stimulus. Teachers and families can work together to assess sensory responses, and use strategies to enhance responses when a student is hypo-responsive and calm them when hyper-responsive. 7. Anxiety Anxiety is not in the DSM-IV criteria, but many people with autism, their parents, and teachers identify it as a characteristic. Sources may include: inability to express oneself difficulties processing sensory information fearing some sources of sensory stimulation a high need for predictability, and difficulty with change difficulty understanding social expectations fearing situations because they are not understood Implications for instruction Programs often need to address anxiety and what contributes to it. Adapt the environment to reduce anxiety-arousing situations, and use a variety of strategies to help the individual manage anxiety and cope with difficult situations.
